summary: This informational memo describes UTF-7, a way of writing Unicode text using only 7-bit ASCII characters, so it can pass through mail systems that handle only ASCII. It also explains its use within MIME.

plainLanguage.summary: UTF-7 writes text in any of the world's writing systems using only the 95 printable ASCII characters that old mail systems understand. Letters and digits appear unchanged, and the rest is tucked into a short run of safe characters marked by a plus sign.

questions: why use utf-7 instead of utf-8 in email
what does the plus sign mean in utf-7
subtitle: A way to write any Unicode text using only 7-bit ASCII, so it survives old mail systems.

tldr.problem: Internet mail carries only 7-bit US-ASCII, but Unicode covers most of the world's writing systems. UTF-8 sends non-ASCII characters as octets in the range decimal 128 through 255, which mail must then encode a second time, bloating non-English text.
tldr.mechanism: UTF-7 writes plain ASCII characters as themselves and wraps everything else in a shifted run: a plus sign, the 16-bit Unicode values in a modified Base64, and an optional minus sign to end the run.
tldr.outcome: The result is mail-safe, readable where the text is mostly ASCII and compact for other scripts. The RFC says UTF-7 should be used only on 7-bit transports such as mail, and that straight Unicode or UTF-8 is preferred elsewhere.

facts.label: Average cost outside ASCII
facts.value: 2 2/3 octets per character plus shift octets

today: RFC 2152 is an Informational memo and is not listed as obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It replaces RFC 1642 and describes UTF-7 as it stood in 1997.

sections.title: Why UTF-7 Exists
sections.content:
Unicode, as defined by The Unicode Standard version 2.0 and ISO/IEC 10646-1:1993(E), defines a character set that encompasses most of the world's writing systems. Internet mail, however, supports only 7-bit US ASCII as a character set. MIME extends mail to support different media types and character sets and could therefore carry Unicode, but MIME neither defines Unicode as a permitted character set nor specifies how it would be encoded.

The problem is that other transformation formats of Unicode, most notably UTF-8, use octets in the range decimal 128 through 255 for characters outside the US-ASCII range. In mail, those octets must themselves be encoded, so the text goes through two successive encoding processes and expands significantly. That expansion puts non-English speakers at a disadvantage: using UTF-8 together with the Quoted-Printable content transfer encoding of MIME represents US-ASCII characters in one octet, but other characters may require up to nine octets.

UTF-7 encodes Unicode characters as US-ASCII octets together with shift sequences for characters outside that range, and one character in the US-ASCII repertoire is reserved as the shift character. Many mail gateways and systems cannot handle the entire US-ASCII character set, so UTF-7 also contains provisions for encoding characters within US-ASCII in a way that all mail systems can accommodate. The memo says UTF-7 should normally be used only in the context of 7-bit transports such as mail, and that in other contexts straight Unicode or UTF-8 is preferred.
sections.plainLanguage: Old mail systems only understand plain ASCII text. To send anything else you have to hide it inside characters they do understand. UTF-7 is one way of doing that, and it keeps most of the message readable to a human or an old program.

sections.title: The Encoding Rules
sections.content:
Unicode here is the 16-bit character set of The Unicode Standard version 2.0. The memo defines three subsets of US-ASCII. Set D, the directly encoded characters, holds the upper and lower case letters, the ten digits, and nine special characters: the apostrophe, the open and close parenthesis, the comma, the hyphen, the period, the slash, the colon and the question mark. Set O, the optional direct characters, holds twenty further characters, including the exclamation mark, the number sign, the dollar sign, the ampersand and the brackets, which may be written directly or shifted; the backslash and the tilde are left out because they are often redefined in variants of ASCII. Set B, Modified Base 64, is the Base64 alphabet of RFC 2045 without the pad character, which is omitted because the only readable encoding for header fields in RFC 2047 is Q, and that encoding already uses the character.

Rule 1 is direct encoding: characters in set D may be encoded as their ASCII equivalents, and characters in set O may optionally be encoded that way, bearing in mind that many of them are illegal in header fields or may not pass correctly through some mail gateways.

Rule 2 is the Unicode shifted encoding. Any sequence of Unicode characters may be encoded using characters of set B when preceded by the shift character, the plus sign, whose ASCII value is decimal 43. The plus sign means that the octets that follow are to be read as elements of the Modified Base64 alphabet until a character outside that alphabet is encountered. Because control characters such as carriage returns and line feeds are not in the alphabet, a shifted sequence always terminates at the end of a line. If the sequence ends with a hyphen, that character is absorbed; other terminating characters are not absorbed and are processed normally. The special sequence +- encodes a literal plus sign, and a plus sign followed immediately by any character other than a member of set B or a hyphen is an ill-formed sequence.

To build the shifted part, each 16-bit Unicode value is first converted to an octet stream with the most significant octet first, and surrogate pairs are treated as two separate 16-bit quantities with no special treatment. Text with an odd number of octets is ill-formed. The octet stream is then encoded with the Base64 algorithm of RFC 2045, modified to leave out the pad character and to add zero bits instead, and when decoding, trailing bits that do not form a complete 16-bit character are discarded, and the sequence is ill-formed if those bits are not zero. Rule 3 allows the space, tab, carriage return and line feed to be written directly, subject to the rules of the MIME content transfer encoding in use.
sections.plainLanguage: Ordinary letters and digits are left alone. Everything else goes inside a run that starts with a plus sign and holds the character values written in Base64 without its padding. A minus sign closes the run, and two special cases avoid ambiguity: the pair +- means a literal plus sign, and a run that ends with a real hyphen needs a second hyphen to close it.

sections.title: Worked Examples and Use in Mail
sections.content:
The memo gives worked examples. The Unicode sequence A, NOT IDENTICAL TO, ALPHA and a full stop, with hexadecimal values 0041, 2262, 0391 and 002E, is encoded as A+ImIDkQ.. The sequence Hi Mom followed by a hyphen, a white smiling face, another hyphen and an exclamation mark, with hexadecimal values 0048, 0069, 0020, 004D, 006F, 006D, 0020, 002D, 263A, 002D and 0021, is encoded as Hi Mom -+Jjo--!. The three Han characters for the Japanese word nihongo, with hexadecimal values 65E5, 672C and 8A9E, are encoded as +ZeVnLIqe-. The text Item 3 is, a pound sign and 1., is encoded as Item 3 is +AKM-1.

The character set UTF-7 is safe for mail transmission and may therefore be used with any content transfer encoding in MIME, except where line length and line break restrictions are violated. Specifically, the 7-bit encoding for bodies and the Q encoding for headers are both acceptable, and the MIME character set tag is UTF-7, which signifies any version of Unicode equal to or greater than 2.0. A message carrying the white smiling face is sent with the header Content-Type: text/plain; charset=UTF-7 and the body Hi Mom +Jjo-!.

For the best interoperability with systems that support neither Unicode nor MIME, line breaks should follow Internet conventions, so lines should be short and terminated with the SMTP CRLF sequence, and the Unicode LINE SEPARATOR (hexadecimal 2028) and PARAGRAPH SEPARATOR (hexadecimal 2029) should be converted to SMTP line breaks. Lines should never be broken in the middle of a UTF-7 shifted sequence, since such sequences may not cross line breaks, so UTF-7 encoding should take place after line breaking. If a line containing a shifted sequence is too long after encoding, a content transfer encoding such as Quoted Printable can be used on the text, or line breaking and UTF-7 encoding can be done at the same time.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of the message stays as plain text. Only the characters that cannot be written directly are replaced by a short run of safe letters and digits, and a reader that knows UTF-7 turns them back into the original characters.

sections.title: What the Encoding Costs
sections.content:
The memo compares what different encodings cost, using assumptions about how often characters from the ASCII range appear in ordinary text. Most Western European languages use roughly seven eighths of their letters from US-ASCII and one eighth from Latin 1, while most non-Roman alphabets such as Greek use about one sixth of their letters from ASCII, the rest coming from their own alphabets, and East Asian languages use essentially all their characters from the Han or CJK area.

For ISO-8859-x in Base64 the average is 1.33 octets per character for all text, and for ISO-8859-x in Quoted Printable it is 1 for US-ASCII, 1.25 for Western European and 2.67 for other text. Unicode encoded in Base64 takes a constant 2.67 octets per character. UTF-8 in Base64 costs 1.33 octets per character for US-ASCII, 1.5 for Western European, 2.44 for some alphabetics and 4 for all others. UTF-8 in Quoted Printable costs 1 for US-ASCII, 1.63 for Western European, 5.17 for some alphabetics and 7 to 9 for all others. UTF-7 costs 1 for most US-ASCII, 1.5 for Western European and 2.67 plus two divided by the length for all others, where the extra covers switching into and out of the shifted form.

The authors judge that UTF-8 in Quoted Printable is not viable, because of the very large expansion of all text except Western European, and that it would only work for texts made of large expanses of US-ASCII or Latin characters with occasional other characters interspersed. UTF-8 in Base64 also has high expansion for non-Western-European users and cannot be read directly even when the content is largely US-ASCII. They prefer one encoding that works reasonably well for all users, and conclude that UTF-7 gives results competitive with ISO-8859-x while giving access to all of the Unicode character set.

As an alternative to UTF-7, the authors consider mixing Unicode parts with other character sets using the existing MIME multipart/mixed content type. Theoretically this removes the need for UTF-7 in message bodies, since multipart may not be used in header fields, but they feel it does not adequately support the intermittent use of specialised characters and short snippets from other scripts that they expect to become common.
sections.plainLanguage: The point of the comparison is fairness. A method that is cheap for English but makes other scripts much bigger is a poor choice for a global network, and UTF-7 was designed to avoid that.

sections.title: When to Use UTF-7
sections.content:
The UTF-7 encoding allows Unicode characters to be encoded within the US-ASCII 7-bit character set. The memo says it is most effective for Unicode sequences that contain relatively long strings of US-ASCII characters interspersed with either single Unicode characters or strings of Unicode characters, because the US-ASCII portions can be read on systems without direct Unicode support.

UTF-7 should only be used with 7-bit transports such as mail. In other contexts, the use of straight Unicode or UTF-8 is preferred. The memo is Informational: it does not specify an Internet standard of any kind, and it replaces the earlier RFC 1642.
sections.plainLanguage: Use UTF-7 when the text has to cross a system that only accepts plain ASCII. Everywhere else, the usual encodings are simpler and better supported.
